common_name: Purissima Bearded Iris (Historic Pure White Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Purissima is a 1927 Mohr-Mitchell tall bearded iris still regarded as one of the finest pure whites ever raised.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Bred by William Mohr from a cross of 'Argentina' and 'Conquistador' and named posthumously by his collaborator W.E. Mitchell in 1927, Purissima bears large, wide-petaled flowers of glistening pure white with a soft lemon-yellow beard, held on tall, well-branched stems. It became one of the most historically important white bearded irises ever introduced, standing behind decades of later white and near-white cultivars including 'Snow Flurry' and its descendants. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, and keep rhizomes in full sun with excellent drainage, since standing water quickly causes rot.

common_name: Thais Bearded Iris (Historic Fragrant Mauve-Pink Cayeux Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Thais is a 1926 Cayeux tall bearded iris still grown as a fragrant heirloom and remembered as a parent of 'Snow Flurry'.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Introduced by the Cayeux nursery of France in 1926, Thais bears vigorous, free-flowering, richly perfumed blooms of mauve-pink to lilac with a white beard, earning a Certificat and Special Prize from the Societe Nationale d'Horticulture de France in 1924. Though eclipsed commercially by later iris, Thais holds a permanent place in iris history as, together with 'Purissima', a parent of the influential white iris 'Snow Flurry'. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, and keep rhizomes in full sun with excellent drainage, since standing water quickly causes rot.

common_name: New Snow Bearded Iris (Historic Award-Winning White Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; New Snow is a 1945 Orville Fay tall bearded iris that was runner-up for the Dykes Medal three years running.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Registered by Orville Fay in 1945 from a cross of 'Snow Flurry' and 'Katharine Fay', New Snow bears midseason flowers described by its originator as neither warm nor cold in tone but simply as white as new snow, set off by a full, bright yellow beard. It earned an AIS Award of Merit in 1948 and an RHS Award of Merit in 1953, and was runner-up for the Dykes Medal in 1950, 1951, and 1952, later passing its clean white color to offspring such as 'Cliffs of Dover'. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, and keep rhizomes in full sun with excellent drainage, since standing water quickly causes rot.

common_name: Cahokia Bearded Iris (Historic Pale Blue Award-Winning Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Cahokia is a 1948 Eva Faught tall bearded iris whose pale blue color and vigor made it an important 20th-century breeding parent.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Bred by Illinois hobby hybridizer Eva Faught from complex seedling parentage involving 'Purissima', 'Santa Barbara', and 'Santa Clara', Cahokia was registered in 1948 and bears clear pale blue flowers of good form and substance, alongside its darker sibling 'Pierre Menard' from the same cross. It received an AIS Honorable Mention in 1949 and an Award of Merit in 1951, and went on to become a foundational parent behind later Dykes Medal winners including 'Whole Cloth' and 'Babbling Brook'. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, and keep rhizomes in full sun with excellent drainage, since standing water quickly causes rot.

common_name: Bluecape Siberian Iris (Historic Bright Blue Violet-Veined Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Bluecape is a mid-20th-century Siberian iris valued as a parent of the Morgan Award-winning 'Swank'.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Registered by British hybridizer Maurice Kitton, Bluecape bears bright blue standards and falls overlaid with fine violet veining on stems to about three feet, a clear, saturated color that made it a popular garden iris and breeding parent in its era. It was crossed with itself to produce the darker-blue 'Canford' and, crossed with 'White Swirl', produced the multi-award-winning 'Swank', giving Bluecape a lasting influence on modern blue Siberian iris lines. Like other Siberian iris it tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and can go many years without division; when clumps become crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

common_name: Trail Blazer Water Lily (Vigorous Bright Yellow Tropical Water Lily)

planting.note: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers in a full-sun pond once the water has warmed well above 70F; Trail Blazer is a vigorous Martin Randig tropical day-blooming water lily grown chiefly for its large fragrant yellow flowers.

directions: Bred by Martin Randig, Trail Blazer is a vigorous tropical day-blooming water lily prized as one of the most reliable bright yellow tropicals in cultivation, producing large, fragrant, sunny-yellow flowers held well above deep green pads. It is a parent of the modern viviparous tropical hybrid 'Innocence' and shares breeding lineage with the popular 'Carla's Sonshine'. Give it a medium to large pond in full sun, since flower production drops off sharply with shade or cool water. As a true tropical it should be grown as a seasonal annual outside zones 9-11 or overwintered indoors as a dormant tuber.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Carla's Sonshine Water Lily (Compact Viviparous Yellow Tropical Water Lily)

planting.note: Plant tubers in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in submerged containers in a full-sun pond once the water has warmed well above 70F; Carla's Sonshine is a compact, viviparous tropical water lily hybridized by Florida Aquatic Nurseries and selected in 2001.

directions: Hybridized by Florida Aquatic Nurseries in 2001 and released to the trade in 2004, Carla's Sonshine is a compact tropical day-blooming water lily bearing deep yellow flowers held close above heavily maroon-mottled pads on short petioles. It is the only widely available yellow tropical water lily that is strongly viviparous, readily producing new plantlets from notches along its leaf margins, which makes it unusually easy to propagate compared with other yellow tropicals. Named by Florida Aquatic Nurseries owner Greg Witstock for his wife Carla, it shares parentage with the white viviparous hybrid 'Innocence'. As a true tropical it should be grown as a seasonal annual outside zones 9-11 or overwintered indoors as a dormant tuber.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Koryu Solomon's Seal (Dragon-Ridge Japanese Fragrant Solomon's Seal)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Koryu is a Japanese selection of fragrant Solomon's seal grown for its raised, dragon-scale-like ridge running down each leaf.

directions: Koryu is a distinctive Japanese selection of fragrant Solomon's seal, its slightly arching stalks set with grey-green, egg-shaped leaves each marked by a raised, gray-green dragon-scale ridge down the center — the trait that gives the cultivar its Japanese name. It emerges unusually early in spring and carries small, dangling, tubular white flowers beneath the foliage, though it is grown chiefly for its unusual textured leaves rather than its bloom. Koryu is the parent of the more compact, faster-multiplying hybrid 'Silver Saddle'. Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, mulching with leaf litter to keep the shallow rhizomes cool, and divide established clumps in spring as the colony fills in.
